newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Steam taken out of NZ dollar rally at close.
newsitem.headline: Steam taken out of NZ dollar rally at close.

text.p: Better-than-expected inflation data and comments by New Zealand First Party leader Winston Peters combined to take the steam out of the New Zealand dollar's rally as it ended sharply lower on Tuesday.

CPI data which showed a 2.4 percent rise over the September year, much lower than expected, sparked a sharp rally in interest rate markets. The currency then fell purely on interest rate differentials.
Comments later from Peters that the New Zealand dollar was clearly too high for exporters knocked the currency about 20-25 basis points lower.

Markets were also less than impressed with Peters' comment that it may take until Christmas to reach a solution to the impasse caused by Saturday's inconclusive election, which left him holding the balance of power between the conservative National Party and Labour.
Adding insult to injury was a wire service report quoting a Goldman Sachs analyst as bearish on the kiwi.
"I guess the market was a bit nervous about the possible prospect of lower rates, although I don't think it's likely," said one Auckland dealer.
"That is a long time to be short Kiwi, so I think people are just nervous on the downside at the moment.
"There has been a bit of a selloff but the market is incredibly short, and I don't think it's going to develop into anything," he said.
The dealer said there was increased nervousness over Peters. "At the end of the day comments like that show he's a bit of a loose cannon," he said.
The Kiwi ended at US$0.6962/67, down sharply from its 0.6993/98 opening and overnight high of 0.7018. The range this session was another wide one of 0.6957-15.
The dealer expected the currency to trade within 0.6940-70 overnight.
One Wellington dealer disagreed the market was short.
"I think a lot of shorts would have been squeezed out on the move back to 0.7018, to be honest," he said.
He expected the Kiwi to trade a 0.6930-80 range overnight.
